standard.title: Music across cultures, times and places
standard.description: explore where, why and how music is composed and/or performed across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have explored music from diverse cultural contexts and discussed preferences (AC9AMU2E01). They can identify where and how people experience music and connect personal preferences to contexts. They have not yet compared music across times and places for similar purposes, or examined audience/performer expectations across different settings.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explore where, why and how music is composed and performed across cultures, times, places and other contexts, comparing purposes, notation formats, performance settings and audience expectations.

nodes.label: Music for similar purposes across different contexts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare music created for similar purposes across different cultural or historical contexts, identifying similarities and differences in how elements of music are used.
nodes.minimum_width: Listen to two pieces created for a similar purpose (e.g. two dance songs from different cultures) and identify one similarity and one difference in how they use elements of music.
nodes.typical_width: Explore music for similar purposes across multiple cultural and historical contexts — dance music, songs communicating identity or health messages, narrative songs; ask questions about rhythmic patterns, instruments and how elements serve the purpose; identify and clap characteristic rhythmic patterns.
wider: Compare music for similar purposes from two different historical periods — how has the instrumentation or style changed while the purpose remained the same?
Explore music from a cultural group in the local community — attend a performance or access a recording and respond by describing what you like, find interesting, or want to know more about

response_modes.reason: Comparative cross-cultural listening is the core task of this descriptor. Each new cultural or historical context adds evidence for both the diversity and the commonality of musical purpose — the pattern that music serves similar human needs in different ways across contexts is only visible with sufficient examples.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparing music for similar purposes across cultures is one of the most pedagogically rich activities in music education — it builds respect for diverse traditions, challenges assumptions about what 'good' music is, and develops analytical listening skills simultaneously.
success_criteria: Can identify the purpose of two pieces of music from different cultural or historical contexts
Can describe at least one similarity and one difference in how elements of music are used

nodes.label: Performer and audience expectations in different settings
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe different expectations for performers and audience members in at least two different performance settings.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one setting where audience behaviour expectations differ from their classroom (e.g. a concert hall vs a rock concert vs a ceremonial performance) and describe what is expected.
nodes.typical_width: Compare performance and audience expectations across multiple settings — when is it acceptable to talk, dance or clap during a performance? What do different settings expect from performers and audiences? Connect these expectations to the purpose of the music.
wider: Investigate a specific performance setting (e.g. a formal concert, a community ceremony, a street performance) and research what is expected of performers and audiences
Compare expectations when experiencing music for ceremony (e.g. a Welcome to Country) with expectations at a school concert — discuss why they are different and why those differences matter

response_modes.reason: Setting-specific expectations are not intuitive to Y3-4 students. Explicit discussion of why different settings have different rules — connected to the music's purpose and cultural context — builds the social understanding of music performance that underpins respectful engagement with diverse musical traditions.

success_criteria: Can describe audience and performer expectations in at least two different performance settings
Can give a reason why expectations differ between settings

nodes.label: Notation and documentation across contexts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore different ways of notating or documenting music and explain how each type conveys information to performers.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify two different notation formats (e.g. graphic notation and a lead-sheet) and describe one thing each format communicates to performers.
nodes.typical_width: Explore multiple notation and documentation forms — graphic notation, lead-sheets (lyrics and chords), staff notation, visual images, music terminology; explain how each conveys different information; connect notation choice to the type of music being notated.
wider: Create instruments from recycled/repurposed materials and use them to create Foley sounds for a soundscape — document the soundscape using an invented notation format
Compare how a staff score and a graphic score represent the same musical ideas — discuss what each can and cannot show

response_modes.reason: Students who have encountered multiple notation formats are better equipped to select appropriate documentation tools in their own composition work. Each format type represents a different philosophy about what needs to be communicated to performers.

success_criteria: Can identify two different notation formats and describe what each communicates
Can explain which format would be more useful for a specific type of music and why
